summary: This informational document offers guidance on developing privacy considerations for protocol specifications. It aims to make designers, implementers, and users of Internet protocols aware of privacy-related design choices. It suggests whether a given RFC needs a privacy considerations section depends on its content.

eli5.summary: People who design internet rules should think about how the rules could expose private information. This is a guide for doing that.

questions: how to write a privacy considerations section
what are privacy considerations in an rfc

subtitle: How protocol designers can spot privacy threats and weigh mitigations, with a questionnaire for spec authors.

tldr.problem: Internet protocol specifications had guidance for security considerations but no comparable guidance for privacy, so privacy-relevant design choices were easy to miss.
tldr.mechanism: The document sets out a communications model, a list of privacy threats, three classes of mitigation (data minimization, user participation, security) and a questionnaire for authors, then works through presence as an example.
tldr.outcome: It is guidance, not a recipe. It says whether an RFC needs a privacy considerations section depends on its content, and it is an Informational IAB document, not a standard.

today: RFC 6973 is an Informational IAB document, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is guidance for analysis rather than a standard, and it does not dictate how to write a privacy considerations section.

sections.title: Privacy Guidance for Protocol Authors
sections.content:
This document is meant to do for privacy what RFC 3552 does for security: give protocol designers a set of guidelines for considering privacy in protocol design. It notes that privacy is a complicated concept with a rich history, often applied to personal data, meaning information relating to an identified or identifiable individual. It draws inspiration from the Fair Information Practices and Privacy by Design, but aims to be more concrete about engineering choices.

The guidance is generic and does not refer to specific legal frameworks. Whether an individual document needs a privacy considerations section depends on its content. Some documents are entirely about privacy, some treat privacy as part of security considerations, and some need no discussion at all. The guidance helps the thought process; it does not tell authors how to write the section.

The RFC also limits its scope. Protocol designers cannot foresee every deployment, and a system's privacy properties depend on the whole system design, the implementation including user interface, and operational practices such as default settings. Designers are asked to consider how a protocol interacts with systems and information outside its bounds, not to imagine every scenario.
sections.eli5: Builders already think about locks on doors. This guide asks the people who design internet rules to also think about who might peek through the windows.

sections.title: The Communications Model and Who Can Watch
sections.content:
The model starts with an initiator that begins communication with a recipient, usually on behalf of an individual whose privacy is at stake. An intermediary such as a proxy, cache or relay may sit between them and is necessary for them to communicate. An enabler helps without being in the path; for example, an HTTP request may be preceded by interactions with an AAA server and a DNS server. Roles can change from one interaction to the next.

Protocol design often assumes recipients, intermediaries and enablers are authorized. Privacy analysis questions that assumption, because such parties can observe, collect, process and transfer data. The RFC groups them as observers, distinguished from attackers by being at least tacitly authorized. An eavesdropper is an attacker who passively observes without the initiator's knowledge.

The terminology section also defines terms such as correlation, fingerprinting, identifiability, unlinkability, undetectability, anonymity set and pseudonym, with many marked with references to RFC 4949.
sections.eli5: When you send a letter, the post office, the mail carrier and the person next door could each see something different. The model names each helper so you can ask what each one gets to see.

sections.title: Privacy Threats
sections.content:
The RFC lists threats drawn from privacy literature and notes that harms include financial, reputational, solitude, autonomy and safety harms. It splits them into two groups.

Combined security-privacy threats are surveillance (observing communications or activities, which can harm even when traffic is encrypted, since traffic analysis may reveal the type of traffic or the protocol in use), stored data compromise, intrusion (such as unsolicited messages and denial-of-service attacks) and misattribution (for example, penalties applied to everyone sharing an IP address because of one abuser).

Privacy-specific threats are correlation (combining information, made easier by persistent identifiers; the RFC shows how TLS session identifiers and tickets sent in the clear can link a resumed session to the original one), identification, secondary use (using data for a purpose other than the one it was collected for), disclosure and exclusion (not letting individuals know about or take part in the handling of data about them).
sections.eli5: Some privacy problems are like someone watching you through a window, and some are like someone collecting your lunch orders over a month to guess your whole routine.

sections.title: Three Kinds of Mitigation
sections.content:
The RFC says privacy is notoriously difficult to measure, but names three classes of mitigation. Data minimization means collecting, using, disclosing and storing only the minimal data needed. Its most direct application to protocols is limiting identifiability, through pseudonyms or no identifiers, and by allowing new or randomized identifiers to be created periodically.

The properties explored under it are anonymity (being indistinguishable within an anonymity set), pseudonymity, identity confidentiality (only the recipient can identify the initiator) and data minimization within identity management. Examples include the P-Asserted-Identity extension to SIP in RFC 3325 and the way EAP methods can hide the username part of a network access identifier from eavesdroppers.

User participation means giving users ways to control and signal how their data is shared and used. Security means keeping data safe at rest and in transit, and the RFC notes that even when confidentiality is achieved, the existence of traffic may still be detectable. Defending against traffic analysis varies by protocol: randomizing packet sizes or timing helps in some cases, while holding them constant is better for real-time communications.
sections.eli5: You can protect a secret by sharing less of it, by letting people choose who sees it, or by locking it up. The RFC says good designs use all three.

sections.title: The Questionnaire for Authors
sections.content:
Section 7 gives guidance as questions about the protocol being designed, useful at any point and particularly after a high-level protocol model exists (see RFC 4101). It does not recommend specific practices because the range of IETF protocols is too broad. It has four groups.

  • Data minimization: which identifiers are used, what other information is exposed, what each observer sees, whether the protocol can be fingerprinted, how long identifiers persist, whether correlation is possible, and what is retained.
  • User participation: what controls or consent mechanisms exist, whether sharing can differ per recipient or intermediary, and whether users can express preferences.
  • Security: how surveillance, stored data compromise, intrusion and misattribution are prevented or mitigated.
  • General: what trade-offs the protocol makes between privacy and other goals, and whether the defaults minimize data, maximize participation and use the strictest security features.
sections.eli5: It is a quiz that designers answer about their own invention: what do you collect, who sees it, who is in charge of it, and how is it locked up?

sections.title: Worked Example: Presence
sections.content:
The example is presence, which lets users see one another's availability. The RFC calls the classical presence architecture nearly a worst-case scenario for privacy design: presentities publish sensitive information to a server, no technical mechanism stops authorized watchers from relaying it, identifiers are long-lived, and users cannot verify who actually receives their presence.

It then considers alternatives. End-to-end encryption of presence runs into usability problems such as discovering watchers' public keys and publishing one encrypted copy per watcher. Redirecting watchers directly to the presentity avoids the server but would disclose the presentity's IP address and is hindered by NATs and firewalls. Because mediation is hard to remove, the IETF work focused on user participation, adding usage indications such as retransmission and retention preferences to location objects so they travel with the data. The RFC says this is an example of thinking, not a model privacy considerations section.
sections.eli5: A presence service is like a friend who tells everyone whether you are home. It is useful, but the friend now knows a lot, so the design adds rules about who may be told.
